Unravel The Story On Climate Change And Social Protection

People face increasingly frequent, severe and complex climate risks that threaten their livelihoods, income security and well-being, making resilience more important than ever.

Choose a country  and scroll down for an interactive storytelling through climate change and social protection risk landscapes that point to the need for climate-resilient social protection.

Section 2.1: WHY CRISP: Climate and Social Protection Risk Landscape

Social protection coverage and climate risks

Social protection will be increasingly critical to building people’s resilience by providing income security before, during and after climate shocks, protecting livelihoods and productive assets, and enabling people to invest in adaptation and diversify their livelihoods. Social protection helps prevent climate impacts from pushing households into, or deeper into, poverty. However, low coverage means that large proportions of households remain unprotected.

INFORM Risk Index (x-axis, higher = higher hazard & exposure risk) and social protection coverage (y-axis, % of population covered by at least one benefit). Bubble area is proportional to population. Population source: World Bank WDI (SP.POP.TOTL), 2025.
How to read the INFORM Risk Index (x-axis)

The index runs from 0 (lowest) to 10 (highest) and reflects a country’s hazard exposure to natural disasters. It does not by itself measure vulnerability or coping capacity — a country further right faces greater physical hazard exposure, regardless of its social protection coverage on the y-axis.

Gaps in social protection coverage leave many people without adequate protection, just as growing numbers are becoming exposed to increasingly frequent and severe climate hazards.

Section 2.2. WHY CRISP: Historical risk landscape

A decade of recurring disasters, and a few stand-out patterns

Sri Lanka has faced climate disasters nearly every year over the past decade (2015–2025):

63%
63%

Floods were the most frequent disaster, accounting for 63% of all recorded events.

52%
52%

Tropical Storm Ditwah in 2025 alone caused 52% of all disaster deaths (823) recorded during 2015–2025, and affected about 1.70 million people.

16%
16%

Drought produced very large exposure despite occurring only twice. The two drought events affected about 1.12 million people — 16% of everyone recorded as affected by disasters over the entire period.

57%
57%

Years 2016, 2017 and 2025 together accounted for 57% of all recorded people affected.

2.3 WHY CRISP: Future climate risks

Future climate scenarios will intensify and increase exposure for people.

If no additional climate action is taken, population exposure to each hazard could look like this.

Data used for this analysis is taken from the NGFS Climate Impact Explorer. NGFS scenarios provide a common and up-to-date reference point for understanding how climate change (physical risk) and climate policy and technology trends (transition risk) could evolve in different futures. Detailed methodology is available in the methodology note. Results of the NGFS Current Policies scenario are outlined below.

Worst case — if we move ahead as business as usual

By 2100, populations will likely be exposed to hazards by:

  • 77.2%wildfire
  • 100%heavy precipitation events
  • 86.9%heat
  • 27.8%drought
Best case — if we achieve Net-Zero goals by 2050

By 2100, populations will likely be exposed to hazards by:

  • 83.9%wildfire
  • 100%heavy precipitation events
  • 0%heat
  • 0%drought
Explore other policy scenarios →

Even with optimistic climate projections, climate change impacts will be part of the future Asia and the Pacific risk landscape. It is critical populations are equipped to meet these challenges and be part of solutions to support climate mitigation and adaptation.

Section 2.4: WHY CRISP: How climate change will impact economic wellbeing

Different climate scenarios will reshape the key indicators that underpin economic well-being.

Climate change policies and events are projected to impact our economies in the following ways:

Key findings — click a card to flip it and see the modelled trajectory

Results displayed here are illustrative outputs of ESCAP macro-economic modelling. Scenario 1a and 1b model a 1-in-50-year flood/drought shock followed by the mitigation effect of post-event policy response. Scenario 2 compares a business-as-usual energy-mix pathway against one that meets primary energy supply and energy-efficiency targets. Scenario 3 compares a benchmark that holds the public transport share at 35% against a pathway raising it to 40% by 2030 and 50% by 2035. Figures shown are illustrative model outputs, not final published results.
Explore more on the macro-modelling methodology paper →

As climate change events and policies increasingly reshape economies and livelihoods, building people’s resilience will require ensuring access to adequate social protection and bringing social protection and climate policies together to anticipate and manage these impacts.

Section 4: How resilient are we?

Amid rising exposure to climate risk, how resilient are populations to meet these challenges?

Section 4.1: How resilient are people?

Looking at 4 dimensions of vulnerability (exposure, vulnerability, coping capacity and capacity to contribute to mitigation), we see who is furthest ahead or furthest behind in access to key opportunities or barriers to build resilience to climate change.

Barrier indicators

Each wedge is one indicator, spanning from the Farthest behind to the Farthest ahead group value on a common 0–100% resilience scale (grey tick = National average). Indicators are split into an opportunity wheel (10 indicators, higher value = closer to resilience) and a barrier wheel (11 indicators, higher raw value = further from resilience). Label colour shows resilience dimension. Hover a wedge for its exact values.
Data is derived from the ESCAP LNOB page. Explore more in LNOB CRISP summary page. 21 indicators are split into those that represent an opportunity to build resilience (where a higher value is better) and those that represent a barrier to resilience (where a higher value signals greater risk), each shown on its own Farthest behind – National average – Farthest ahead radial scale. Indicator label colour shows its resilience dimension (vulnerability, coping capacity, mitigation, exposure).

Understanding who is furthest behind is only part of the picture. We also need to examine whether the policy landscape is equipped to close these gaps, build people’s resilience and enable them to contribute to climate action.

When social protection and climate change policies are better aligned, they can build resilience of people to climate risks and enable people to contribute to climate action.

Strengthening synergies between social protection and climate policies can ensure that climate action systematically builds people’s resilience, while social protection systems are equipped to respond to evolving climate risks. Bringing these policy areas together can harness social protection’s established systems and policy tools to protect people from growing climate risks while enabling them to adapt and contribute to climate action.

Subtitle Section 4.3. ARE WE READY? Key findings from CRISP

CRISP analysis with the Government of Sri Lanka highlights gaps and opportunities in the policy environment to guide the way forward.

The CRISP study in Sri Lanka points to five priority actions — click a card to see what each involves:

1. Make social assistance climate-responsive and scalable

Click for details ↓

Use existing programmes, including Aswesuma, to incorporate climate-related vulnerability into programme design and delivery, with the ability to temporarily increase benefits and expand coverage to households affected by climate shocks.

2. Strengthen risk-informed identification and data systems

Click for details ↓

Use the Social Register alongside disaster, meteorological, exposure and livelihood information to support dynamic identification and reassessment as vulnerabilities change, supported by interoperable systems and strong data governance.

3. Link early warning systems to anticipatory social protection

Click for details ↓

Use hazard and forecast information to trigger predefined social protection actions, financing and delivery arrangements before losses are fully realised, enabling faster and more effective responses.

4. Expand protection and resilience for climate-vulnerable workers and households

Click for details ↓

Strengthen protection for informal and climate-exposed workers through stronger links between social security, insurance, employment, skills and productive-inclusion programmes, while connecting income protection with climate-resilient livelihoods.

5. Integrate social protection into climate action and implementation

Click for details ↓

Position social protection as a key mechanism for climate adaptation by linking it with climate planning, climate finance and implementation processes, supported by strong coordination, gender responsiveness, data governance, and continuous testing and learning.

Assessing the readiness of social protection and climate policy systems helps identify where stronger linkages, capacities and policy responses are needed to build people’s resilience and chart practical ways forward.
